blocks.text: Now, if we may run through the passages of Scripture about this serpent, the first is Prov. [col. 403] XXIII, 32., where Solomon says of wine, At the last it bites like a serpent, וכצפעני יפרש, and stings like a tsiphoni (or basilisk). This is not to favour Tatian, the Encratites and the Manichaeans, who called wine the gall of the dragon and the poison of the ancient serpent, and abstained from it even in the Holy Supper. For here it is not the use of wine but its abuse that is condemned. God by wine makes glad the heart of man, Psalm. CIV, 15. Indeed wine is said to cheer both God himself and men, Iud. IX, 13., namely in the sacrifices, in which it was used, Exod. XXIX, 40. and Num. XV, 5. Some, however, would have the word אלהים elohim in that passage signify not the true God but judges and magnates, as in Exod. XXI, 6. and XXII, 8. 9. 28. and Psal. LXXXII, 6.; to these would be opposed אנשים, men, that is, commoners. In the same way, in Gen. VI, 2. the sons of men are opposed to the sons of God, and in Psal. LXXXII, 6. 7. אדם (that is, man) to gods and sons of the Most High. The sense would then be that by drinking wine rich and poor, princes and subjects, judges and clients are cheered alike. This is exactly what the first of Darius's bodyguards says of wine in 3 Esdr. III, 19. 20. However that may be, the yield of wine is ascribed to God's goodness and liberality, Ierem. XXXI, 12. and Os. II, 8. And the Israelites are promised the early and the late rain, that they may gather in their grain and wine, Deut. XI, 14. And a cluster of grapes, brought into the wilderness, served them as a sample of the fertility of the land of Canaan, Num. XIII, 24. Nor should it be said that what had been promised and permitted under the Law was forbidden under the Gospel. For Christ, invited to a wedding, changed water into wine to be offered to the guests, Ioh. II, 8. He himself drank wine many times with the Apostles, and at that Last Supper he even consecrated it to be the sacrament of his blood for the whole church. What is more, Paul recommends to Timothy the use of wine for his stomach's sake, 1 Tim. V, 23. But here a thing good in itself is condemned because of the evils of drunkenness. If anyone does not weigh these sufficiently, let him, like the boys of the Lacedaemonians, look at a drunken man: his disordered face, his tottering feet, his stammering tongue, his ungainly gestures, and his reason blinded and moved from its seat. Let him likewise consider the bleary eyes of gluttons, the nose suffused with bile, the rotten teeth, the foul breath, the trembling limbs, and the belly distended with fat; not to mention paralysis, gout, vertigo, convulsions, lethargy, apoplexy and a thousand swarms of diseases. However grave these are, they bring more disgrace than pain, because they are not accidental but self-inflicted, and are ascribed not to the weakness of nature but to the force of intemperance. Moreover, when reason is drowned in drink, the depraved passions are kindled. Hence Solomon, Prov. XX, 1.: Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness [III, 188] riotous: whoever delights in it is not wise. And Prov. XXIII, 29.: Who has woe? Who has evoë? Who has contentions? Who has babbling? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Those who tarry long at wine, etc. And below ^{a)}: Your eyes shall look upon strange women, and your heart shall utter perverse things. Thus by such cups men are changed into beasts. Some into lions: like Alexander, who killed Clitus, the dearest of his friends, over the cups; and Herod, who, leaving a banquet, consigned a servant of God to death. Others into dogs: like Nabal, who, full of wine, barked at David. Others into swine, who wallow in foul pleasures: like Lot, who, when drunk, defiled himself by incestuous intercourse with his daughters. In short, by other vices the image of God is extinguished in us, but by drunkenness and gluttony even the image of man. Indeed, we are cast down below the cattle, which do not drink except when there is need, nor stir up thirst by art, but follow nature as their guide. Since, then, drunkenness is pernicious in so many ways, wine is not undeservedly [col. 404] said to bite us like a serpent and to sting like a basilisk. Will sting in Hebrew is יפרש, with right-hand Sin. Elsewhere this word means to arrange or to scatter; here it means to sting, from the Chaldee language ^{(1)}, in which פרש peras is an ox-goad and פריש paris is a spur. Hence among the Hebrews too פרש paras is a horseman, who pricks his horse with spurs. But the verb פרש with left-hand Sin means to spread out. With this in view Jerome rendered, As a regulus it will spread poisons, and the Greeks, Ὥσπερ ὑπὸ κεράστου διαχεῖται αὐτοῦ ὁ ἰός [Hōsper hypo kerastou diacheitai autou ho ios]: As by a cerastes its poison is spread ^{(2)}. But the Chaldee and the Syriac have here, As a basilisk דפרח, which flies, as if they had read יפרח for יפרש ^{(3)}. This would be quite absurd, for no one mentions a flying basilisk. Far be it from us, then, to add wings to such a monster, which is so terrible by its creeping alone. According to the first version, At the last it will bite like a serpent, and sting like a basilisk, the two hemistichs are thoroughly ἀντίστροφα [antistropha]. For as serpent and basilisk, so to bite and to sting are nearly the same.
